components.text: Whether avoiding unexplained emergence establishes consciousness as the uniquely preferable foundation.
Whether cited empirical compatibility discriminates idealism from a neutral alternative.
The decisive demand is whether rejecting matter-to-consciousness emergence uniquely warrants consciousness as the sole foundation.
The empirical considerations must distinguish idealism from a neutral alternative rather than merely remain compatible with it.
How idealism can preserve an observer-independent ordered external world rather than merely private qualities.
How the proposed dissociation model itself is justified.
The decisive demand is to explain how idealism preserves an external ordered world rather than merely replacing physical vocabulary.
Whether describing the inaccessible represented reality as mental adds an explanation of its structure.
The decisive demand is whether calling the represented external substrate mental explains its structure and the origin of representations.
How idealism explains representation, organism boundaries, causal interaction, and predictable order.
Why consciousness-first ontology is preferable to neutral monism.
The decisive demand is to explain representational construction, organism boundaries, and predictable causal order within idealism.
The earlier demand is to show that idealism adds explanatory value beyond merely avoiding material emergence.
Whether eliminating a physical category requires making universal consciousness the remaining substance.
Whether phenomenal character belongs to represented objects or to representations.
The decisive demand is whether avoiding the hard problem requires the idealist category or can be achieved through neutral representation.
Whether placing phenomenal character in representation avoids the need to explain why that representation is experienced.
The decisive demand is whether representations can account for phenomenal character without presupposing an experiencer or experiential ontology.
A further demand is whether idealism adds explanatory content beyond changing the substrate label.
Whether experience can persist outside the narrative self-model and across other informational complexes.
Whether representations presuppose phenomenal subjectivity rather than explain it.
The decisive demand is whether experience persists outside the narrative self and how subjective character is distributed among informational models.
The broader demand is whether representations alone suffice without an antecedently experiential ontology.
Whether IIT's integration measures explain why an informational complex has any subjective perspective.
The decisive demand is whether IIT explains why integrated information or an excluded complex has any subjective character.
What IIT must establish if its role here is operational prediction rather than metaphysical explanation.
The original demand asks IIT for metaphysical explanation; the replacement demand is whether its operational mapping makes measurable predictions.
Whether IIT's causal-complex language supports any ontological conclusion about existence for itself.
The decisive demand is whether IIT's complexes explain phenomenal existence or merely encode causal and informational organization.
Which subject or complex bears causal power when the personal self is conceded to be constructed.
How a subjective perspective is individuated from the unstable ego model.
The decisive demand is to identify the bearer of causal power when represented content is not autonomous and the personal self is unstable.
What subject remains when the personal self dissolves and can serve as the bearer of experience.
The decisive demand is to identify the subject underlying experience and causal activity once the narrative personal self is dissolved.
How the universal-subject account locates the immediate causal source in an ordinary dream without a distinct self.
The decisive demand is whether universal subjectivity actually locates the cause of particular dream contents when no personal self appears.
Where causal regularity comes from if neither the dream object nor an experienced personal self is fundamental.
What deeper entity bears the causal dispositions attributed to the personal “I.”
The decisive demand is to locate causal regularity when neither the dream object nor a represented personal self supplies it.
The earlier demand is to identify the ultimate bearer of causal powers after the ordinary self is rejected.
Whether talk of fields, vibrations, frequencies, and processes covertly presupposes space and time.
Whether altered experience supports a nonspatiotemporal universal subject.
The decisive demand is whether field, vibration, frequency, and process language covertly depends on fundamental space and time.
How structured differentiation and meaningful relations can persist without fundamental spatial or temporal extension.
The decisive demand is to preserve meaningful differentiation and structure without treating ordinary space and time as fundamental.
